text: Chapter 1's terraform plan showed you exactly what would change before terraform apply touched anything real. Bicep and ARM have that same safety check, through az deployment group what-if, and a newer feature called Deployment Stacks closes a real gap that plain Bicep and ARM deployments have always had: by default, Azure never deletes a resource just because you removed it from the template. This lesson covers both — previewing changes safely, and managing a deployment's full lifecycle instead of only ever adding to it.

az deployment group what-if, run with the same resource group, template file, and parameter file you'd use for a real deployment, evaluates your Bicep against what's actually in Azure right now and lists every change before anything happens. Each resource gets a symbol: plus for create, minus for delete, tilde for modify in place, equals for no change — the same information terraform plan's own plus/minus/tilde markers give you, just produced by ARM instead of Terraform's state engine. Run it before every real deployment.

Here's the gap: Azure deployments run in incremental mode by default, which only adds and updates resources that are in the template — it does not delete a resource just because its block disappeared from the template. That resource keeps running, orphaned. Complete mode does delete anything in the resource group not present in the template, but that's dangerous at resource-group scope: it deletes everything unmanaged, not just what your own deployment previously created. Terraform never has this problem, because its state file already tracks the full set of resources it's responsible for.

Deployment Stacks track precisely which resources a deployment created, and az stack group create takes the same template and parameter file you already have, plus an action-on-unmanage setting: deleteResources cleans up specific resources dropped from the template or from the stack itself, deleteAll also removes the resource group, detachAll just stops tracking without deleting anything. Update the stack by rerunning the same command with the same name against an updated template, and resources removed from it get cleaned up automatically — the outcome Terraform state already gives you by default.

What-if previews a deployment and Deployment Stacks manage its full lifecycle, including real cleanup — both real, current Azure capabilities. Next lesson closes out this chapter: an honest comparison of Terraform and Bicep, and the real factors that decide which one fits a given project.
